thread.title: It starts with a seed

author: gqlshare
title: It starts with a seed
text:
If you take a walk through the natural beauty of Nolde Forest, French Creek State Park, or even your own backyard this early fall, you’ll notice a shift. The vibrant blooms of summer are slowly giving way to dry seed heads — the brown pods of milkweed, the bristly cones of purple coneflower, and the fluffy seed heads of asters and goldenrods.
To the untrained eye, these fading plants signal the end of the garden season. But to a growing movement of Berks County home gardeners, they represent something far more exciting: possibilities!
A single native plant can produce hundreds of seeds. By harvesting and planting them, you aren’t just growing a garden, you’re building a vital pitstop for migratory birds, butterflies and overwintering pollinators and ensuring that next year’s insects will have their needed food source.
When you collect seeds from plants that have thrived in Berks County’s specific clay soils and weather patterns, you are preserving ecotypic seeds — genetically adapted local strains that are far more resilient to regional weather swings.
Some of the fun of seed collecting is figuring out where to find the seed and what it looks like. There are seeds found in pods that can be easily pried open with your fingers (false blue indigo — baptisia australis) to those that are best smashed with a rolling pin (foxglove beardtongue — penstemon digitalis).
There are seeds that catch the wind with their pappus or fluff and float away (New York ironweed — vernonia noveboracensis). Other seed heads hide their seeds away in calyx tubes or chambers until they are coaxed out by turning the seed head upside down and tapping (wild bergamot — monarda fistulosa).
And some seeds just like creating a challenge for us by forcibly ejecting their seeds long distances when ripe (jewelweed — impatiens capensis). A small organza bag placed over the dying flower can capture these seeds.
Fall is the time to collect the vast majority of native seeds. At this time of year, carry around a few small bags, a pair of nippers, and a marker. A seed head should be brown, crunchy and dry to the touch with at least an inch of the stem, brown and dry as well, to ensure the best chance of collecting viable seeds. Harvest seeds on a dry day after the dew has evaporated and before they burst open or are blown away on a windy day.
Seeds can easily be cleaned by removing the chaff or excess plant debris by using a common household sieve or using winnowing techniques by breaking down the seed head with your hands and gently blowing the chaff away.
Once cleaned, store harvested seeds in paper bags or on paper plates for 1-2 weeks to dry thoroughly. Dried seeds can then be stored safely in glass or plastic containers in a cool, dark and dry location. Don’t forget to label the container. As much as we hate to admit it, our memories will fail us now and again.
Nature has everything figured out. Sometimes we just need to provide a little help. Part of that help, when it comes to seed saving, is understanding how seeds germinate.
Many of the seeds native to Pennsylvania enter a dormant state to prevent them from sprouting prematurely on warmer winter days. They require a prolonged period of damp, cold weather, typically 30 to 90 days, to trigger germination. This process used to eventually break dormancy is called stratification.
Some seeds require seed scarification, which is needed when certain species have a hard seed coat. In nature, these seed coats are worn down by winter’s freeze and thaw cycles, soil abrasion, or passing through the digestive tract of wildlife so they can absorb water and grow.
By understanding these natural means of seed survival, you can help by using techniques at home like winter sowing in milk jugs, nicking the seed coat with a file or placing seeds in a cold-moist environment in your refrigerator to stratify your seeds to mimic nature.
Any conversation about seed collecting should include the need for ethical seed saving. Since most plants provide a bounty of seeds, you need only collect sparingly, taking no more than 10% of the seeds, leaving the rest for wildlife and natural reseeding and make sure to ask permission when collecting on lands that are not your own.
Some of the fun of seed collecting is figuring out where to find the seed and what it looks like. (Courtesy of Dee Dee Kerscher) Identifying the plant is crucial to not only knowing that you are helping to propagate a specific plant but that you also are not contributing to the spread of invasive species.
To a casual observer, while walking along a stream, a plant, resembling a large woody shrub, catches your eye with stunning plumes of white flowers that are buzzing with honeybees collecting nectar. So why not come back in the fall and collect some seeds, right? Please don’t!
This could be a stand of Japanese knotweed, a known invasive species that is extremely destructive and outcompetes our native flora leaving our native bees lacking essential food sources. A quick check of state invasive plant lists before gathering wild seeds ensures you are propagating helpful natives rather than inadvertently spreading destructive invasive species.
Now you have collected your seeds for the year, make sure to share your yield with friends and neighbors at the Berks County Master Gardener’s Community Seed Swap on National Seed Swap Day, Jan. 30, 2027, at Berks Nature.
This is where we come together as a collective energy to ensure that native plants will survive from year to year providing seeds for birds and the genetic substrate for future pollinator generations.
More information on seeds, seed collecting, seed storage, hybridization and heirlooms, germination, and planting can be found by contacting the Master Gardeners at Penn State Extension of Berks County. 610-378-1327 or berksmg@psu.edu.
Sandy Weiss is a Penn State Extension of Berks County Master Gardener volunteer.
